extracted.intended_audience: historians, anthropologists, and historical demographers reconstructing aboriginal population sizes from documentary and ethnographic sources (ethnohistorians)
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and evaluative principles for reconstructing pre-contact and early-historical native population sizes using Spanish expedition diaries, mission records, ethnographic lists, material evidence (horses/meat), and spatial inference. Emphasizes correction factors, cross-checking observers, and conservative rounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use primary Spanish expedition and missionary accounts as core data
rubrics_metrics.description: Base counts and descriptive data primarily on diaries and lists from Spanish visitors (e.g., Estudillo, Moraga, Munoz, Pico) and mission baptism records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat carefully recorded counts (e.g., Estudillo's warrior counts) as strong evidence; extract village names, warriors seen, visitors, chiefs, and any numerical statements (e.g., Moraga's '5 rancherias ... 250 almas'). Use these as starting points for aggregate estimates and cross-checks with later ethnographers and mission registers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert counted warriors (or warriors seen) into total population by applying observed warrior:total ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: When only numbers of warriors are recorded, infer total inhabitants by applying empirically observed ratios of warriors to total population (examples: Estudillo's counts; Latelate ratio 79 warriors → 200 total → ~2.5:1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the same ratio observed at well-documented villages to similar groups when appropriate. Example: Estudillo saw 437 'jovenes de arma' and other counts to infer village and regional totals. State the specific ratio used and justify by analogy to comparable cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust for visitors, retinues, and festival congregations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that some recorded counts include visiting groups at fiestas or chiefs with accompanying retinues, which can inflate local population figures if interpreted as resident totals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate resident village population from visiting contingents (e.g., Estudillo saw 600 visitors from the 'roblar' and seven chiefs with retinues); estimate visitor retinues proportionally and avoid double-counting. Example calculation: assume ~114 persons per visiting chief retinue and allocate accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for fugitivism and flight-induced undercounts
rubrics_metrics.description: When observers state that people fled on approach (common in early expeditions), recorded counts likely underrepresent true population sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the diary notes that 'most fled' or only warriors remained, increase estimates relative to the observed numbers or rely on other sources (lists, reports from locals). Example: Moraga's party often encountered fleeing natives; where the 'List' gives larger numbers than the diary, prefer the larger or reconcile the two with an upward correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct modern/ethnographic village counts upward to estimate pre-contact (aboriginal) values
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that village populations remembered by informants or recorded circa 1840–1850 were often reduced from aboriginal levels due to disease, raids, and disruption; apply a retention/correction factor (e.g., ~70% retention) to estimate precontact population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use regionally appropriate multipliers: the text uses ~70% (i.e., divide observed by 0.7) for Mono and Miwok to reach aboriginal estimates; elsewhere the author ascribes a one-quarter reduction (i.e., multiply by 4/3) for heavily disrupted groups. Justify choice of factor from local evidence and analogous areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impose minimum plausible village size under normal (aboriginal) conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: When village counts reported are improbably small (e.g., <15 persons), assume a conservative minimum (e.g., 20 persons) for pre-contact conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increase very low reported values to the minimum threshold before further extrapolation (example: in Gifford's list, villages with 15 or fewer were raised to 20 persons each). Document these adjustments explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust persons-per-family and houses-per-village figures to reflect aboriginal family sizes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use houses-per-village and informant family-size numbers, but increase family-size estimates to account for probable larger aboriginal families (example: raise Gifford's family number 4.89 to 6.0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute mean hamlet/village size from (houses per hamlet × families per house × persons per family), adjusting family size upward for aboriginal conditions and including previously-used but now-empty houses when relevant (e.g., include remembered unused houses to estimate former occupancy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mission baptism records to scale tribe sizes
rubrics_metrics.description: When mission baptism totals are available for a subgroup, infer total tribe size by multiplying baptisms by an empirically justified factor (example: 246 baptisms at Soledad → infer tribe ≈ 1,000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify the multiplier (e.g., baptisms may represent a quarter of the tribe) based on mission catchment patterns and contemporary comparisons; state uncertainty clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use material/consumable evidence (e.g., killed horses/meat yields) as indirect population indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Counts of animals (dead/live horses) and estimated meat yields can constrain minimum group sizes needed to use or preserve those resources (example: 200 horses → 120,000 lb meat → would feed 329 people one pound/day for a year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convert animal counts into caloric/weight units, apply plausible per-capita consumption/preservation assumptions, and derive lower- or order-of-magnitude population estimates. Use such calculations as confirmatory or bounding evidence, not precise counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply spatial proportionality (population per river mile) for poorly documented stretches
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume approximate proportionality between riverbank distance (mileage) and number of inhabitants where rivers and habitats are ecologically similar; compute persons per river mile and extrapolate along comparable sectors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divide well-documented sector totals by airway miles to get persons-per-mile (examples: lower Merced 1,750 over 32 miles → 55 persons/mile; middle Kings 5,000 over 75 miles → 67 persons/mile) and apply to analogous river sectors. Treat this as an approximate method; check against other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer conservative estimates and round to convenient units
rubrics_metrics.description: When uncertain, choose conservative (lower-end) values and round aggregate totals to nearest hundred for reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author consistently rounds to nearest hundred (e.g., 7,600 → reported as 7,600; many regional totals rounded to 3,500, 9,100 etc.) and notes uncertainties. Explicitly state rounding conventions and reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-validate with multiple independent lines of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on a single source type; reconcile Spanish expedition counts, ethnographic village lists, mission records, archaeological/ethnohistorical indicators (horses), and later informants to form a coherent estimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where sources disagree (e.g., Moraga's low figures vs. later ethnographers), evaluate observer reliability and use convergence or weighted judgment. Document reconciliation steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate observer reliability and systemic bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether particular observers tended to under- or overestimate (e.g., Moraga's figures were 'uniformly at variance' and often too low) and adjust trust weighting accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider context (first expedition, frightened natives, fugitivism) when assessing counts. Prefer carefully conducted counts (e.g., Estudillo's methodical pacing and counting) over casual or flight-affected reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for intermittent occupancy and multi-period house counts
rubrics_metrics.description: When informants recall extra houses no longer occupied, include remembered unused houses in reconstructing aboriginal occupancy levels (example: add 44 formerly used houses to active hamlets to estimate past houses-per-hamlet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish active occupancy from remembered past occupancy; include both appropriately when estimating prehistoric populations, especially for intermittently inhabited groups like the Mono.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use regional ecological comparability to transfer inference factors
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying correction factors or persons-per-mile calculations, ensure the areas compared are ecologically and habitationally similar (e.g., Merced and Kings river habitats compared to Fresno/Chowchilla sectors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit transfer of multipliers to sectors with similar riverine habitat and village spacing; note when analogies may not hold and increase uncertainty accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly state and justify all assumptions and corrective additions
rubrics_metrics.description: Make visible any arbitrary assignments (e.g., adding five persons to each village, assigning 500 to unspecified villages) and provide the rationale or conservatism behind them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the text include adding five persons to villages thought to have experienced reduction, assigning 500 to other villages arbitrarily when documentary evidence is sparse, and assuming 250 per rancheria when reconciling lists. Record these assumptions so readers can re-evaluate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use demographic residue checks (survivors vs. aboriginal totals) for plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare mid-19th-century survivor counts to reconstructed aboriginal totals to see if decline percentages are plausible (examples: survivors ~23.7% of aboriginal in Kaweah basin; lower-river comparable values ~17.2%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If derived decline percentages are wildly inconsistent with nearby regions or documented epidemics/raids, revisit assumptions. Use survivor ratios as a sanity check rather than a primary estimator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat festival/aggregation counts carefully — they may reflect supra-local populations
rubrics_metrics.description: Large gatherings (fiestas) can bring together people from many rancherias and should not be counted as the population of a single village; use festival counts to estimate the size of the wider regional population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Estudillo's observation of 600 young men and 200 young women as visitors was used to infer populations of the Kaweah/roblar region (estimating that 600 young men represented ~1,700 persons). Allocate visitors back to their home districts proportionally when estimating regional totals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot and measure village spatial dimensions and convert historical units when available
rubrics_metrics.description: When observers provide village dimensions in historical units (varas, leagues), plot to scale and convert to modern equivalents to estimate area and compare to urban analogues (e.g., city blocks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Estudillo's semilunar village measured 624 and 756 varas on sides → plotted to give area 80,000 square varas; assuming Spanish vara ~ yard and city block ~300 feet, the village equated to ~eight city blocks. Use such spatial measures to support population-density judgments.
